title: Three chains, no loops

prereqs.why: Every chain here borrows its input rather than consuming it, which is why they all take a slice.
The longest word of an empty list is None, and the compiler will not let you forget it.
All three functions take &[T], so the same code works on a Vec, on an array and on part of either.

statement:
Read `n`, then `n` integers, then any number of words.

Write these three functions and use them:

```rust
fn evens_squared_sum(xs: &[i64]) -> i64
fn longest(words: &[String]) -> Option<&String>
fn running(xs: &[i64]) -> Vec<i64>
```

- `evens_squared_sum` is the sum of the squares of the **even** values.
  An empty slice gives 0.
- `longest` is the longest word. On a tie, the **last** one of the
  longest wins. An empty slice gives `None`.
- `running` is the running totals: the `i`-th entry is the sum of the
  first `i + 1` values. An empty slice gives an empty vector.

Then print exactly:

```
evensq <the sum>
longest <the word, or the text none>
running <the totals, space separated>
```

The `running` line is printed even when the list is empty, with nothing
after the word.

### The sample

```
5
1 2 3 4 5
alpha be gamma
```

```
evensq 20
longest gamma
running 1 3 6 10 15
```

### The constraint

**Write each function as a single expression — one iterator chain.** No
`for` loop and no `mut` accumulator inside them. That is the exercise:
the standard adaptors already do all three of these jobs.
hints: `xs.iter()` gives an iterator of `&i64`, so the closure parameters are references. `filter` hands you `&&i64`, which is why you will see a `*` in the condition.
`.filter(...).map(...).sum()` is the first one. `sum()` needs to know what it is summing to, and the return type of the function tells it.

For the longest word, `max_by_key(|w| w.len())` is the whole function. On a tie it returns the **last** maximum, which is what the specification asks for — `max_by_key` is documented to do exactly that.

For the running totals, `scan` is the adaptor that carries a value along: `xs.iter().scan(0i64, |acc, x| { *acc += x; Some(*acc) }).collect()`. Returning `None` from the closure would stop the iteration early, which is not wanted here.
